going to enter upon a period of peace. But the policy of the department did not vary a great deal. Gradually its estimates were cut down. We hardly know what the defence policy of this country is supposed to be. Now it would seem as if we are going to be called upon to join in a race in armaments. Again I am not speaking merely of our own government but I point out that our own government is apparently contemplating something of this kind, and unless some direction is given by the house I do not see how the department can very well avoid travelling in that direction. In a recent issue of the Montreal Gazette, January 31, 1934, I notice an account of an address given by Major-General McNaughton, in which he told of some of the newer and more efficient weapons, and he concluded thus:
In history, we are not long concerned with nations unable or unwilling to keep pace with armament developments. However notable their civilization, however brave their warriors, and however adept their statesmen in the art of treaty-drafting, they soon pass from the stage before the onward march of those well able to forge and wield the newer weapons.
So to-day apparently the chief of staff is preparing to provide us with more recent and more efficient weapons. I presume that that is his job as chief of staff, but I would say that it is the job of this parliament to say whether that is the way we propose to defend this country.
I noticed the other day a very interesting article in Canadian Business, which is published by the Canadian Chambers of Commerce, from which I will read a few sentences:
Canadian business men are no strangers to war in the past tense. Too many of those we knew fought and died. All glory to them and credit to those who have returned to carry on. So much for the past. The future is an entirely different matter. Canada, doesn't want another war, but if there should be one, Canadian business will have to foot the bills. As our friends "The Extremists" have told us, war is much too expensive, even though it is far from impossible. If you don't believe it, let's look at some costs-then think until it hurts before entering another.
In the good old days a true sword in the hands of an able man was an excellent and economical military investment. Then along came gunpowder, and with it the customary cost budget: two bullets equalled one fatality. However, as we entered the machine age, warfare became its apt pupil and best customer. Result: it now costs $25,000 to kill a soldier.
That is from the business standpoint. I think we are all beginning to realize the terrific cost of war. We cannot very well look over the world situation to-day, whether
in Europe or in Asia, without realizing that another war is quite a possibility. So it seems to me that we, as a nation, have to decide very definitely what action we should be prepared to take, and how we plan to defend ourselves. Are we simply going to enter upon this armament race, as the nations have done again and again in the past, or is it possible for us to devise some other means by which we can contribute alike to the safety of the world and to our own security? I think that is the question which ought to be faced by this house. It ought not to be sufficient for these estimates to be presented and for us to discuss whether or not we want another camp here or a militia unit established somewhere else; those are questions which undoubtedly will have to come before any advisory committee on defence. Rather it is for us to consider the main policies and what is necessary under those policies.
The other day I came across this statement, which very well opens up the whole question:
I appreciate the seriousness of the statement that I am about to make to this honourable house, but I am giving my considered, definite opinion when I say that I cannot conceive of any developments which would justify this country in sacrificing the blood of one single Canadian on the future battlefields of Europe. Let us look ahead! We must! We generally get into trouble by not taking the long view. Let us act in such a way that we can honourably decline to participate when the hour arrives.
That was said by a prominent Canadian military man in another place, and I believe that statement places the situation squarely before us. Whence are we to look for security? Are we in Canada to adopt an isolationist policy; are we to say that we must prepare to defend ourselves against all comers and that through our own unaided efforts, by means of our military equipment, our great navy and our air force, we are to protect our coasts? Is that to be our policy? In all seriousness I submit that if that is our policy the amounts we are voting in these days are altogether inadequate. I am not urging larger appropriations, but I do say that if we propose to depend upon our own unaided efforts to defend our coasts through military strength, then these sums are insignificant; they are wholly inadequate for such a purpose.
What other policy might we possibly adopt? We live alongside a very powerful neighbour, the United States. Are we to depend upon the United States for defence? I can understand that we may need to do so if trouble should break out between, we will say, the United States and Japan. Therp is quite a .

possibility that if the United States were attacked Canada would be attacked also, and what is to be our position in such a contingency? Are we to be prepared to withstand such an attack alone, or shall we have to fall back upon the military strength of the United States?
Again, it may be said that we are members of the British Empire, and that we will have to depend upon the British navy. I am not sure whether under certain circumstances the British navy would be an asset or a liability, or whether the British navy could be counted upon to come to our assistance. And I have enough independence to say that if we are going to take that position I could almost join with those who say we ought to make our contribution to the British navy, a policy in which I do not believe as I hold to another policy altogether. I do admit, however, that those who definitely depend upon the British navy to protect us have a great deal to support them when they advocate that Canada ought to make her contribution to the British navy.
Let me point out that our connection with Great Britain might easily lead us into troubles that we as Canadians otherwise might escape. Great Britain has a far-flung empire; trouble might break out in India, in Hongkong, in the islands of the sea, in the nearer east, in Egypt or in any one of a hundred places where Great Britain has interests. Under those circumstances what is to be our attitude as a Canadian people? Are we prepared to do our share in the defence of the empire, and to come to its defence as we did in 1014? I think those are questions that ought to be pretty clearly stated. If Great Britain should be depending upon Canada coming to her defence again, as she did in 1914, and if this statement which I have read expresses the views of many Canadians, then it seems to me we might be letting Great Britain down pretty badly at a crucial time. If Canada is not in the future to send a single soldier to die on the battlefields of Europe, we should be prepared to make the statement honestly and openly to the public, and let the world and the British Empire know where we stand in that regard. But we have not done that. Are we then, in planning for national defence, taking these matters into consideration? If we take the stand that we will not come to the help of Great Britain if she becomes involved in some European or Asiatic turmoil, now is the time in all honesty, to say so, and if we say so we cannot expect help from Great Britain.

There is one other relationship that I think ought to be recognized. We are a member of the League of Nations. Does that mean anything to us?
No.

Somebody suggests that it does not mean anything; I am not sure whether or not that is an official pronouncement. If it is, I think that official pronouncement ought to be given very wide publicity. The League of Nations means nothing to us; then, I ask, what is the alternative? The League of Nations, at least in ideal, has stood for a collective system of maintaining peace. I have never been enthusiastic over the League of Nations, because at first it was very largely a league of victors, and throughout to a large extent it has been a league of great powers. None of us was willing to grant the league any very great measure of power; too often we have asserted that we would maintain our own sovereignty no matter what happened to the league. Well, the league has done some good pieces of work, but the league has shown itself very weak indeed because the member nations would not give the league support, and to-day the League of Nations is very much discredited. But having said all that I come back to this point: what, then, is the alternative? If we are going to give up the idea of an ordered world, of peace and of agreements as a means of attaining peace; if we are to go back to the bad old way of fighting it out as individual nations, where will the world be within a very short time? If that takes place, war, and a much more serious war than the last, is inevitable, and that in the not distant future. It seems to me that if we were serious about the League of Nations we would spend a great deal more of our energies in trying to work out, through the league, some of these world policies which might bring us peace. Apparently we are not very active in that. And so we are in this House of Commons and in this country flopping backwards and forwards without any definite policy.
I venture to raise this question to-night in the hope that it might stimulate us to do some thinking. Are we prepared to defend ourselves by our own efforts against all comers? Secondly, are we going to ally ourselves with the United States? Thirdly, are we going to maintain our connection with Great Britain, and under what conditions? What obligations are involved in the maintenance of that connection? Then, fourth, are we to emphasize our membership in the League of Nations and either make that league something worth

I would say this,
that often one has to choose between two alternatives. If, instead of each nation maintaining its own force, and all armed to the teeth, we had some sort of international air police service, we might be taking a very decided step in advance. But, personally, I confess that I have very little confidence in physical force as a means of settling disputes. Within the bounds of the nation we have set up courts and most of us obey fairly well the decisions of the judges in those courts. I think we will not be on a safe basis until we come to
some such arrangement in our international affairs, set up our courts and all agree to abide loyally by their decisions. That would be civilization. I do not know whether we can attain that position at one jump, but in the meantime I believe in working as rapidly as possible in that direction.
I do not intend to detain the committee further, but I think I am justified in asking the minister to give to this committee some idea as to the underlying policies of our national defence. I think I have a right to ask that, and I hope we may have some statement from the minister.

I suggest that the government should be commended for the stand it has taken in regard to national defence. Practically every nation in the world believes in defence. The great trouble which has occurred in the past, and has come down through the centuries is that some strong and powerful nation has. become so refined and over-civilized that it has refused to fight or to support itself and has deputized other people to do its work and fighting, with the result that some other, stronger and more virile race has come in and conquered. There is a great tendency for civilization and the desire nob to fight getting too far advanced in this country. I do not believe in a nation of nincompoops who will not stand up for themselves. It is only the, lowest and most depraved sort of man who will not under certain circumstances defend himself. I believe the same holds true as regards a nation. Canada has to be prepared to defend herself to take her place in a manly and proper way in any world affair which may develop.
The hon. member may pick up any newspaper and read of difficulties throughout the world. We find in practically every paper we read that in Europe, in Asia and in South America there are very serious difficulties. What can we do but be prepared to defend ourselves if the necessity arises, or to take a proper part in the solution of any difficulties?
The hon. member spoke about the League of Nations. During the difficulties which occurred a year ago in Manchuria the great difficulty with the League of Nations was that it did not have a force. If the League of Nations is going to do anything and gain anything I think finally there has to be behind it some measure of force. Canada is a member of the League of Nations, and we must be prepared to carry our share of the load. At the present time we have not a force which is at all out of the way. Our permanent force consists of about 3,500 men, which acts as the nucleus, and then there is the non-permanent militia, a very highly trained and efficient force. It is able to deal with anything that may happen inside the country. Some unpleasantness might arise at any time in any part of the country, and it is the duty of the provinces to keep peace within their borders so that the people may pursue their ordinary vocations unmolested. The first duty of any nation is to maintain law

and order, and we have not one man too many to support the provincial police and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police when called upon. We were called upon once this year. Fortunately we did not have to do anything in particular when we got there, but the small force that was sent did have a restraining influence. Such an incident might occur at any time, and if we did not have an efficient force sufficient in numbers to support the provincial authorities when called upon to help maintain the civil power, this government would not be doing its duty.
The permanent force also is prepared to train the non-permanent force, which, if the necessity should arise, could be expanded as it was in 1914. I hope just as strongly as does the hon. gentleman that there will never be any occasion to use the force, but if there is I want to see the Canadian militia, permanent and non-permanent, prepared to do its part.

Then am I correct in inferring from the minister's reply that our army exists very largely to maintain order within the country and that no provision is being made to defend Canada against external enemies?

One of the main
duties of a government is to maintain order within its borders. At the present time, of course,, our permanent force is not large enough to go overseas; that is not its object, but nobody can foretell exactly what an army is going to be used for. The force is there to be used for some legitimate end should the occasion arise.
I should like to ask the minister on what 'occasion was the permanent force called out during the last year?
Stratford.

The hon. member is about as logical as she usually is. We were asked by the provincial government to turn out the force, and acoording to the law of the land it was our duty to do it in aid of the civil power.

I do not wish to unduly delay the minister's estimates, but I wish to make a few observations arising out of the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with respect to camps in which unemployed are used in preparing landing fields for aircraft. With the position taken by the hon. member that the feeding, housing, clothing and payment of these men at twenty cents a day is not a satisfactory solution of unemployment conditions I think no hon. member will take issue, and certainly I shall not, but I do wish to refer to the inference to be drawn from or pointed to by his objection that these camps are being operated under the Department of National Defence. From that the hon. member went into a discussion of war and expenditures of money on war; and he asked if these men were put into the camps under the department for the purpose of having them handy for use-
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to misinterpret my remarks. I said and implied nothing of the kind.
I accept the explanation of my hon. friend, but I did gather that he objected to these men being used for unemployment purposes under the Department of National Defence.
I thought the camps ought to be under the Department of Labour.

I know that when these camps were first started it was stated, and published very widely, and the agitation gained considerable force in this country, that these men were in camps under the Department of National Defence and were being subjected to military discipline. I think my hon. friend made reference to that.
I said nothing whatever to-night about military discipline.

Military
supervision, perhaps my hon. friend said.
Mr.. WOODSWORTH:	Quite so.

My hon.
friend draws pretty fine distinctions. What is the difference between military supervision and military direction?
I am sure that the hon. gentleman as a former soldier knows that there is a vast difference between the two.

Well, we
shall not go into that. So far as these camps being under the Department of National Defence is concerned1, and being under military supervision or military direction or military control, there was much propaganda throughout this country to the effect that that was the condition. I took occasion to investigate the matter. I am sure that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre had knowledge of that propaganda. I wonder whether he ever took the trouble to investigate how much military control or military supervision there was.
I tried to.

And if my hon. friend found the facts to be as I learned them to be, would it not have been just as well, would it not have been fair since he raised the question, to state here to-night what were the facts he found as to these camps? It was commonly stated1 that these men first had to be attested; secondly, that they were under military direction or military control. It was further stated that it was done by the government, under the guise of giving unemployment relief, actually for the purpose of having at hand and readily available the young manhood of our country to meet any emergency that might arise. The facts are that these men were not attested. They were under no military discipline or control. There are always some facts that can be coloured and distorted to give an appearance of truth in propaganda. The papers that these men were required to sign, the form they filled out, was readily available. Thousands of men were being taken into these camps, and surely the first duty of any man in charge of a camp is to know who are the men in that camp. What are their names? Are they married or single? Whence do they come? All these details were taken, and that is all there was to that. There was no attestation.
As to being under military direction, it is true that the camps come under the Department of National Defence. But the men in charge of the camps were not men in uniform. There were no rifles, no bayonets, no machine guns-nothing of the sort. These camps are

Supply-Dejence-Reliej Camps
similar to the ordinary lumber camps. They are comfortable and modem. Discipline is left to the men themselves and to their foremen, and that is the best kind of discipline you can get. The men are as free to leave as they are to enter. When a men receives word of placement in civil life he is provided with his return railway fare. If he be there a short time and desires to leave without having been placed in civil life, he is free to go. The food conditions, the clothing conditions and the shelter conditions are of the best. These men work for their food, shelter and clothing and in addition receive twenty cents per day and some other articles. I agree that these camps do not offer a satisfactory solution for unemployment, but I do not think there is anything sinister in the fact that they are being operated by the Department of National Defence. The question may be asked: Why by the Department of National Defence and not by the Department of Labour? It happens that the Department of National Defence is the only department which has in its employ engineers who are trained in construction work. These camps are carrying out important public undertakings in the construction of landing fields for aeroplanes and it was necessary that these fields should be prepared in a proper way under the direction of engineers. The engineers of the department could see that the work was properly carried out and an economy was effected in not having to hire other personnel.
From the reference made from time to time to things military, some hon. members would indicate that we should apologize for the estimates of the Department of National Defence. What is behind it all? Is there any reason why Canada should apologize for having a department of national defence? We are not a warlike people. I am one of the most peaceful of persons, but I cannot subscribe to the doctrine that we can ensure peace to the people of Canada by emulating the ostrich, burying our heads in the sand and crying "peace, peace," when there is no peace. I am glad that we have the League of Nations. I believe it has accomplished much more than it is generally given credit for. But back of the League of Nations is the idea that force may be necessary to enforce the treaties of that league. I was a little surprised that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) did not give a straight reply to the question asked by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland). He was asked whether or not he was in favour of using force to back up the treaties of the I Mr. W. W. Kennedy.]
League of Nations. I think we must face the question. We do not want force, but we are not living in "the best of all possible worlds." We have to take things as they are; we must be practical. What purpose is served in this house or in the country by assuming that the estimates of the Department of National Defence should be apologized for? I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) and to all those who cry "peace, peace," when there is no peace: Remember that the history of our race and of every race is that prosperity is only for the free and that freedom is the heritage of those alone who have the courage to defend it.
I wish now to deal briefly with the purpose of the work being carried on in these camps and upon which these young men are being employed. They are preparing aircraft landing fields across Canada. Are these being prepared for purposes of war? No. They are being prepared preeminently for the purposes of peace and the expansion of trade and commerce. We all know what an extra day means commercially in a journey by sea; we all know what a few hours mean in mail transportation and in the delivery of commercial papers such as contracts and that sort of thing. The future of trade and commerce lies in the development of air transportation. The greatest air route in the world lies across Canada. This is envisaged to-day; it will become more obvious as years go by. The path of commerce in the air from Europe to North America and across the Pacific lies across Canada. This path is not south but north of the forty-ninth parallel of latitude. The most direct route westward from Europe to Asia is across Canada north of the St. Lawrence. This government is to be commended for the work which has been already done in laying a foundation for a transatlantic and trans-Canada route. Canada's future as one of the great trading nations of the world is bound up in aeronautics. The Americans have investigated this matter and have explored our north country. The recent northern flight of Colonel Lindbergh was not one of idle curiosity. I do not propose to go into that this evening but I should like to do so on some other occasion. Other nations have attempted to obtain vested rights to the air routes across Canada. My best information is that the work on these landing fields was started only after careful study and with the object of laying the foundation for a trans-Canada air service.

These young men who have been taken from the ranks of the unemployed are performing a real national service. In my opinion there has been no work undertaken in Canada in the last decade as important as this establishing of an air route across Canada. I would like to see those men paid more than twenty cents a day and I hope the government, taking note of the better times coming that we hear so much about and which I firmly believe are indeed here, will at the earliest possible moment, which cannot be too soon, on works suoh as these employ men at a normal wage, because to my mind they are contributing to an undertaking that is transcendentally important in the development of Canada. I think Canada should be able to afford to pay and should pay men employed on work of such national importance a reasonable living wage.

Recently
there has come to me from away out on the prairies, from a farming community far from any village or town or city, word that an active canvas^ is being carried on by people, whether they be C.C.F.'s, communists or socialists, I do not know, but they are all regarded as one and the same thing in that locality, to use the word "revolution" whenever possible in order that our people may become accustomed to the term. Imagine such a thing!
I judge from the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) to-night and from the many speeches which he has delivered in the house, that he has evidently come to the conclusion that the proper way for him to bring about war is to talk war, war, war, trouble, trouble, international trouble and every other kind of trouble. There is not a single trouble known to the human race, internationally or in any other way, that the hon. gentleman has not brought up in review in the house in the last three or four years. He is a constant trouble hunter; in fact he is running a trouble factory, and if he wants trouble, he will get it. We in Canada are a peaceable people: we do not want war; we do everything we can to prevent war. If you go to the Chateau Laurier amongst the war veterans in session there, you will not find a single man among them who is not opposed to war, and we on this side are actively opposed to war, but if the hon. gentleman stirs up trouble and is hunting for it, he will get it and he will be very sorry for it.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Macmillan) was talking about the camp in his
constituency. I have only one objection to that camp. It is not in my constituency and it is taking hundreds of men from the city of Regina, so that to that extent they are being taken away from us. I would like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to tell me this: If the young men are so dissatisfied ; if the camp is so badly run, so abominable as he desires to make out, why is it that dozens of young men, sons of mothers and fathers living in towns and not eligible, are coming to me and asking me to get them into that camp? Does he think they want to get into a dungeon or into filth or into poverty? I do not think so. They want to get into that camp because they know they will be well taken care of and well fed. I have been in those camps and I know something about military life. I do not know whether my hon. friend ever was in military life or not, but I was, and from my observations of those camps they are the best run institutions that can be found anywhere. Certainly there is discipline, but it is in order that the men may be well fed and well looked after. Some of them, as a matter of fact, are too well fed because it is apt to make them think 'the state is going to continue to keep them when it is not. We are simply carrying them through this condition of depression. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he become a league of nations unto himself and give us some peace in this House of Commons.

May I be permitted to answer the question asked by the last speaker? He asks why these young men would go into the camps, why they were coming to him wanting to get in. It is because they had not enough to eat if they did not go in and because it is too cold for them to wander around. I think that is quite a good answer.
I would like to ask the minister whether out of the five dollars a month or twenty cents a day that the men get, they have to provide their own clothes, or are their working clothes provided by the government?

When they go into a camp, the understanding, indeed the fact is, that they are clothed, fed, sheltered, and given an allowance of twenty cents a day. That is in no way a salary, and it is not, as some hon. members have said to-night, with the idea of keeping them there. We do not want to make it a wage. This is not a permanent affair at all; it is merely a transition stage until those young men can get back to work.

I could not tell exactly. I mentioned this afternoon that there might be some from Montreal, some from Sherbrooke, and some from other towns round about.
How do they happen to get into these camps?

The qualification for a man to get into these camps is that he is single, homeless, unemployed and physically fit. Anyone in that category in the city of Sherbrooke would apply to an employment agency, either provincial, or dominion if there is one there; or to the mayor or the relief officer of the city. The district headquarters would be communicated with, and if there was a vacancy at the nearest camp he would be sent there. Has the department any plan for some day taking these men out of the camps? How do they intend to rehabilitate them in the ordinary life of the country?

We endeavour in every way possible to encourage the men to get back into civilian work, and with a good deal of success. From the camps in Ontario already 2,069 have left the camps and gone to assured positions. In Quebec 1,366 have gone back to work; in New Brunswick, 211; in Nova Scotia, 337; in Manitoba, 54; in Saskatchewan, 172; in Alberta, 48; and in British Columbia 1,123 have left camps to go to positions.

I will put the question
this way: A lady came to me the other day and asked me if I could intercede to get a certain young man whom I know, of good character, a splendid fellow, into the position of chauffeur to a certain person in one of our cities. The man would leave the camp with perfectly good clothes; if the man he was going to work for wanted to get him into a livery, he would have to buy it himself.

Are they in military

I know there are

Well, Mr. Chairman, we
are hearing the annual criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to the relief ;amps. I am pleased to support any activity which looks forward to an increase in aviation services, because I believe hon. members realize that on the whole, in her *national development Canada has perhaps gone farther in aviation than any other country. It is a matter of pride to me that in past years we were able to vote something like $5,000,000 in connection with forestry patrol, geological surveys for mining work, fishery patrols and other services in order to develop our civil aviation. I believe the minister has that in mind, because I understand the other day he delivered an address in Toronto which showed he was familiar not only with the needs but with the possibilities of aviation in Canada.
How much work has been done at Bishopton and up to date how much money has been expended?
I regret to say I have not before me that information, but I can get it for the hon. member.
May I put the question in this way: Is the work far enough advanced so that landing would be possible, or has only the preliminary work been done?
I cannot give an accurate answer to that question. About two months ago I saw some pictures of the field, and at that time it certainly did not look as if it could be used.
In addition to the clearing of sites for airports, what other general work has been carried out by the camps? Is it the intention of the government to keep those camps open during the summer months?

In addition to the airport work, the camps in British Columbia did a good deal of work on the roads. Then, there is the citadel in Quebec and also the one at Halifax which are badly in need of repairs. Those are two historic landmarks in Canada, in connection with which a good deal of work has been done. Then there is some



Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
forestry work; for instance, the Lac Seul project is very largely one of forestry. The one we have in New Brunswick ait Coulter's Siding is a forestry project, and finally will be used as a camp for that district.
In the summer months?

In the summer months, if necessary, we will keep them open. Last year we found that a large number of men went away, particularly in western Canada, and worked in the harvest, or at one thing and another. They will be kept open, but we encourage the men to go out and get other work if they can.
What was the cost per day of feeding the men at different camps?
The men are on regular army rations. It costs 29-2 cents per day.
That is the figure for the whole of Canada?
Yes, that is the average.
Has the minister the figure for the province of Quebec, with particular reference to Valcartier or Quebec citadel, as compared with the costs in British Columbia?
I have not that information before me, because my figures are the averages.
But the minister could furnish those figures?
Yes.
Has the minister any idea of how much it costs to clothe a man in the winter season?
It costs for clothing 18-7 cents per day.
It would be difficult for me to answer that question, because I have not the figures in front of me.
I imagine there must be a schedule showing the clothing issued to the men.
Yes.
Does it include underwear and that sort of thing?
Yes; they are very well provided with clothing, such as warm mackinaws, underwear, socks and rubber boots. At the present time lumbermen's boots are used.

I have
listened with a good deal of interest to the discussion which has taken place to-night, and being of a curious turn of mind I cannot help remembering 1930. It is most interesting to see the way in which hon. members opposite come to the rescue of the government in carrying out the policy which they promised in 1930 to put into effect if they were returned to power. I for one am greatly interested in seeing the development of that policy and the defence of it that hon. gentlemen opposite attempt to make. I am sorry the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) found it convenient to leave, also the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MacMillan) as well as other hon. gentlemen opposite who rushed to the defence of this policy of the government to cure unemployment. How comforting it must be to the people of Canada to realize that now we have the real policy of the Conservative party on unemployment expounded to us by these gentlemen to-night, together with the statement by the minister who is administering the relief camps for the single, homeless unemployed men! How comforting it must be to the electors who voted for these gentlemen! I look at the promises that were made by the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) and by his followers in all parts of Canada not only to cure unemployment but to end it, and yet nineteen thousand young unmarried men are being taken care of by the government of Canada in the various camps to which reference has been made. I have no fault to find with the administration of these camps by the Department of National Defence or with the treatment of the men, but what must the men themselves think? A fair percentage of them voted to put this government in office to end unemployment, and what must they think when they find themselves employed in this manner? Surely the Conservative party ought to be proud of its record. And remember that in every town and village of any size in Canada married men are on direct relief, thirty per cent of which is contributed by this government. And yet hon. gentlemen opposite fly to the rescue of the minister because some criticism is offered by

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and by the lady member of this house (Miss Macphail) over this state of affairs. It is not good enough to say that these conditions are common to every country, because hon. gentlemen opposite said that if they were put into office they would cure unemployment and find work for all. But they did not say it would be at twenty cents a day. They never mentioned twenty cents a day, nor did they say they were going to put the single unemployed men into relief camps and give the dale to those who were married. The hon. member for Long Lake, for instance, tries to ridicule the hon. member for Winnipeg North' Centre for his attitude. It is a sorry spectacle to see hon. gentlemen opposite have to admit after four years of office that this is the best they can do for the unemployed in Canada. What a spectacle!
Deplorable!
Let us be serious for a moment.
I am quite serious, just as serious as the hon. gentleman's leader was when he was making those promises to the electors in 1930.

My hon. friend is not serious or he would not have said that the hon. member for Saskatoon ridiculed the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when actually he paid him a compliment by addressing him as the right hon. gentleman.
I never said anything of the kind, and if my hon. friend would only sit and listen he would know what I am saying.
You deliberately said that he ridiculed the hon. member for Winnipeg.

Will the
hon. gentleman kindly speak when he gets the opportunity? I do not wish to put on record again, as I had intended to do, the promises made by this government, not only by its leader but by his followers, to cure unemployment in this country. Had they said then that their method of curing it was to be the method that they are defending to-night, they would not be sitting where they are now, in the seats of the mighty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What would have happened the country then?
No titles.

What would have happened? If my right hon. friend can 74726-98J
suggest anything worse than the present condition I should like to know it. If the right hon. gentleman is proud of the record of his government he is welcome to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, he certainly is.
Then I say to him that I am very glad he makes that statement because the people of Canada are anything but proud of him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would compare popular approval with the approval of the hon. gentleman.
No doubt you will have to give us the opportunity and we will let the public decide. When we have to take our medicine we take it, and you will take yours on the next occasion.
That is your supposition.
Is it? All right. I say again, Mr. Chairman, that I did not rise to criticize the administration of the relief camps.
Oh, oh.

He laughs best who laughs last. I did not rise to criticize the administration of the relief camps. I believe they are well administered, but I do say that it is a sorry spectacle for the government of Canada that the relief camps should have to be established at all, and it is not an answer to say, as has been said on former occasions, that it is the result of world conditions, because hon. gentlemen sitting opposite over there are the ones who promised the electors of Canada that if they were put into office they would cure unemployment-and this is the way you have cured it. Are you proud of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

Proud of the situation that exists to-day? Proud of the number of unemployed? Proud of the steps you have taken to deal inadequately with the situation? Then if you are, you are much more case hardened than I thought you were.
Give us the promises that were made.

In Halifax, the right hon. gentleman who now leads this government made a speech on July 4, 1930, in which he said:
If the Conservative party comes into power on July 28th I propose at the earliest moment to call parliament together so that we may find speedy remedy for this situation and decide on means to provide work for Canadians. Work I said, not doles.

Supply-Dejence-Relief Camps
That is plain enough, isn't it? And yet we have in the neighbourhood of one million people-or that was the number-a very large proportion of whom are on doles and nothing else. And this government is not doing what it promised to do, to take care of the situation as a great national emergency, because it is paying only thirty per cent of the dole.
Then at Moncton the leader of the Conservative party said:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date after July 28, and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole. . . . Mr. King promises consideration of the problems of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
I have not heard anyone from Moncton or thereabouts get up to-night and speak of the wonderful way in which that promise has been carried out.
Again, speaking at Ottawa, the right hon. gentleman said:
Mr. King promises you conferences; I promise action.
Is there any government that has outdone this government in calling conferences during the past three years? And what have been the results of them all?

Your leader has been
complaining that we did not call enough conferences.

What has been the result of it all? Absolutely nothing. We have a wheat agreement by which we reduce our production by over one million bushels. That is the result of one of the conferences.
Then, speaking at Renfrew, the right hon. gentleman said-and I am sorry that the hon. member for Renfrew is not now in his seat, because he must have been present at this meeting, otherwise it could not have taken place:
I will enact such tariff measures to give Canadians an even chance, or perish in the attempt.
This was a real perishing government before they got into office. He went on:
At the same time we will protect labour as well as consumers. There will be no exploitation.
We now have the Stevens committee sitting day after day and discovering how labour has been exploited under the very nose of this government.

Mr. CAiSGRAIN: The higher the tariff, the lower the wage.

I do not know what steps may be taken to prevent labour from being exploited, but that is what is being found out in another room in this building. Such a thing should make every Canadian blush with shame, but all this was going to be prevented by this government. These are the promises by virtue of which hon. members opposite sit in the seats of the mighty.

Give us some more
of them.

There are
too many, and I do not want to clutter up Hansard. Then they wonder why criticism is offered when we have before us estimates to provide relief camps. I marvel at the nerve of the government, and I wonder how they are able to face the people after making such spacious promises. I repeat that it is no use saying to hon. members on this side and to the public generally that it was world conditions that brought all this about. They knew about world conditions in 1030, but they stated that it was the fault of the government of that day that there were 117,000 unemployed in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, what is the
number of this vote? I have lost my place.

Perhaps the hon. member will find his place some day. I do not wonder he has lost it, and I am afraid he will lose it a good many times if he attempts to follow the intricacies of this government. We are discussing unemployment and relief camps. Does my hon. friend realize that we are talking about relief and the cure of unemployment?
Twenty cents a day.
I was just wondering.

I have no
particular fault to find with the twenty cents a day, but I say without fear of contradiction that these conditions have been brought about by the policies of this government. If this government said in 1030 that world conditions had nothing to do with the situation then existing, how can they argue to-day that world conditions are causing the unpleasant situation we have in this country? They cannot swallow themselves; that is impossible, although they will try to do it.

They blow and swallow at the same time.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

They do not like this sort of thing. I know it does not go down with them. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) was very laudatory in his statement about these camps. He told us how splendidly they were 'being conducted. With all of that we agree, as we know that anything undertaken by the Department of National Defence will be well done. But I say again, is it not a sorry spectacle that Canada, having such great undeveloped natural resources, should have to operate unemployment camps in order that men may obtain sustenance and a reasonable amount of clothing? Is it not a sorry spectacle that this is what has to be done under the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite?
What will happen under the policies of the Liberal government?

When the
Liberal government come into office their policies will be enunciated. May I say to my hon. friend that he was in a very happy and comfortable position under Liberal policies. We did not have any relief camps and we had mighty little unemployment. ,
You would not have given a nickel if you had.

We did not need to give nickels; the government provided employment for all. Even the tobacco growers down in Essex were able to get along without relief, the same men for whom the hon. member is pleading so hard to-day. This government was going to blast its way into the markets of the world, but my hon. friend is to-day asking for relief for those very men who were to benefit from the policies of the government. Are you proud and pleased with your record? Hon. gentlemen on the back benches opposite will rush to the defence of the government. They are ready to advocate relief camps and other forms of unemployment relief, notwithstanding the fact that they declared solemnly to the electors that they would not inaugurate such things. They are welcome to all the comfort they can get. That is all I have to say in connection with this matter.

Would the hon. member
kindly tell the committee just what he would do? Has he any constructive suggestion to offer?
Change the government.

Tell the committee so the
public will know just how you would deal with unemployment.

I would
deal with it in exactly the same way as the Liberal government dealt with it in 1922. I would bring about the same era of prosperity which was brought about in 1922 by the application of Liberal policies. That is the way I would deal with it, not by trying to blast my way into the markets of the world and shutting the gates to all whc wanted to get into Canada. The government's policies have been on trial for four years and each year the conditions have become worse than they were in the previous year. The one man of those who occupy the front benches opposite for whom I am sorry is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). He has to try to raise revenues while the policies inaugurated by the present government are being carried out. He has made a dismal failure of it and is bound to make a dismal failure so long as these policies are followed.
Progress reported.
